companyInfo.Industry: Health Care: Pharmacy and Other Services

description: Headquartered in Woonsocket, R.I., CVS Health owns the country’s largest pharmacy chain with more than 9,000 physical locations found mostly in the Northeastern U.S. The publicly traded corporation is comprised of more than 300,000 employees and offers pharmacy services, health and beauty products, convenience foods, and other services like photo printing. CVS Health didn’t start adding pharmacies to new stores until 1967, but since then has acquired large companies in the health space such as Aetna, Signify Health, and Oak Street Health to boost its primary care offerings and develop its own insurance arm. Other subsidiaries of CVS Health include benefit services manager CVS Caremark and MinuteClinic, a walk-in health clinic for vaccinations, health screenings, and other quick appointments.

title: CVS Health

rankings.title: Fortune Global 500
rankings.itemDescription:
The health retail, pharmacy, and insurance conglomerate is the largest company ever to be led by a female CEO; Karen Lynch has been chief executive since Feb. 2021.

  • CVS exceeded Wall Street’s revenue expectations in 2022 with $322 billion, but profits fell nearly 50% compared to 2021.

  • The company made progress in expanding into the primary care space with two big acquisitions: primary care network Oak Street Health, purchased for approximately $10.6 billion; and health services company Signify Health, for approximately $8 billion. The deals were completed earlier than anticipated, prompting the company to lower its earnings expectations for 2023.

  • CVS joined other health care companies in settling lawsuits that claimed they should have known they were filling too many opioid prescriptions. Under a settlement announced in December, CVS will pay state and local governments up to $4.9 billion over 10 years. (The company did not admit wrongdoing.)

The health retail, pharmacy, and insurance conglomerate led by Karen Lynch is one of the nation’s two biggest health care companies. It’s also the biggest company ever to be led by a female CEO.

  • CVS exceeded Wall Street’s revenue expectations in 2022 with $322 billion, but profits fell nearly 50% compared to 2021.

  • The company made progress in expanding into the primary care space with two big acquisitions: primary care network Oak Street Health, purchased for approximately $10.6 billion; and health services company Signify Health, for approximately $8 billion. The deals were completed earlier than expected, prompting the company to pull back on earnings expectations for 2023.

  • CVS joined other health care companies in settling lawsuits that claimed they should have known they were filling too many opioid prescriptions. Under a settlement announced in December, CVS will pay state and local governments up to $4.9 billion over 10 years. (The company did not admit wrongdoing.)

rankings.title: Fortune Global 500
rankings.itemDescription: CVS outpaced analyst expectations for 2021 under the leadership of Karen Lynch, who came aboard as CEO in February. The company reported $292 billion in revenue for the fiscal year ended December 2021—an 8.7% increase year over year. In a quest to revolutionize America’s access to health care, Lynch initiated a plan to transform hundreds of CVS stores into super-clinics that provide primary care—creating what will become the nation’s biggest network of urgent care and primary care outlets. CVS also played a major role in fighting COVID-19, administering over 50 million vaccines and 29 million tests through December 2021. In the fight to retain talent, CVS announced a minimum wage increase to $15 an hour, effective July 2022.

rankings.title: Fortune Modern Board 25
rankings.itemDescription:
CVS, the retail and pharmacy giant that ranks fourth on the Fortune 500, scored high on gender equality, board independence, and ESG. Karen Lynch was named CEO in February 2021 and has said the company is “pivoting to become more central to America’s health care.” The company recently made the decision to raise its minimum wage to $15.

CVS counts the former CEOs of Chiquita Brands; AT&T; Becton, Dickinson; Johnson & Johnson; PCS Health Systems; and Applied Biosystems among its directors. The board also has two members with high-level government experience: Nancy-Ann DeParle is the former deputy chief of staff and director of the White House Office of Health Reform, and Mary Schapiro is a former chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Editor's note: An earlier version of this post misspelled the name of Nancy-Ann DeParle.

rankings.title: Change the World
rankings.itemDescription: CVS-owned Aetna last year launched an effort to reduce suicide attempts. Its clinicians began asking mental health screening questions of most members, rather than querying only those who showed risk of self-harm; it also reached out to high-risk youth. Aetna has seen an 18% decrease in suicide attempts since 2019 among its 16.3 million adult members with behavioral health coverage—a promising start.

rankings.title: Fortune Global 500
rankings.itemDescription: CVS embedded itself on the front lines of the COVID pandemic as one of the central hubs for distributing vaccines to local communities. In the first quarter of 2021 alone, the company, now fully integrated with health insurer Aetna following a mammoth $69 billion acquisition, produced more than $69 billion in revenues. In 2020, revenue grew $12 billion compared to the previous year. Karen Lynch, who became CEO in February 2021, believes that “millions of new customers will engage with CVS Health for the first time through testing and vaccine administration.” The company’s upbeat guidance for 2021, meanwhile, relies on pharmacy sales, rather than retail, to carry the revenue growth.

rankings.title: Fortune Global 500
rankings.itemDescription: The drug store chain-slash-health care juggernaut got a $62 billion revenue boost—due to its $69 billion acquisition of Aetna, the insurance giant, in 2018. Though investors haven’t entirely sweetened on the deal, CEO Larry Merlo pronounced the integration of the two companies “successful” in February. Former Aetna CEO Mark Bertolini, meanwhile, resigned from the CVS board and said the integration was “far from over.” As a pharmacy retailer on the pandemic’s frontlines, CVS’s sales were brisk in the first quarter, but Merlo has warned about the “uncertainties” that surround the long-term performance of the company’s multifaceted business in a time of COVID-19.
